output.title: Before-and-after framing hides the middle
output.body:
The quiet cost of before-and-after framing is that it makes a workflow look cleaner than it is. A small business owner sees “before manual invoicing, after automation” and gets asked to trust the gap without checking the middle. But the middle is where the real decision lives: setup time, learning curve, integration friction, and the handoff from demo to daily use. That is where the story turns into work.

For a bounded Bareni decision, I would not start with “Will AI do it?” I would start with one recurring workflow and ask whether it is repeatable enough to test. That is what the free 30-minute diagnostic is for: identify the one recurring workflow, say honestly whether AI fits, and, if it does, define pilot scope, fixed price, and measures. The point is not to promise an outcome. It is to separate a paper before-and-after from a working one.

A practical next step is simple: write down one process you repeat every week and the measure you would accept as success before you commit. If you cannot name that in plain English, the “after” is still a story, not a decision.

The real before-and-after test happens inside your workflow, not in a vendor demo.
